articles.summary: Xiaoqi Zhou harshitha.rv@f… Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:53 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Shanghai, China, supporting clinical research sites across mainland China, with a particular focus on East, West and North China. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have been working in clinical research for approximately four years, gaining experience in clinical trial operations and supporting studies from start-up through execution. What is the best part of your job? What I enjoy most about my role is the opportunity to continuously learn and challenge myself while contributing to the development of new therapies that may ultimately improve patients' lives and support the approval of innovative medicines. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of the most fascinating aspects of clinical research is seeing how a study protocol is translated into real-world practice. No two sites operate in the same way and every patient brings a unique perspective and experience. Each study provides new insights into disease biology, regulatory requirements and the importance of effective patient communication. I have also been continually impressed by the resilience, motivation and knowledge of many clinical trial participants. Patients often arrive well informed, ask thoughtful questions about treatment options and safety, and demonstrate a genuine commitment to advancing medical research. What are you most proud of in your work? I am proud of the role I play in protecting the integrity of both science and clinical practice. Every document reviewed, every process completed and every protocol deviation prevented contributes to the quality and reliability of the research. For me, clinical research is about much more than procedures and data. It is about honouring the trust that patients place in us and helping generate evidence that may benefit future patients around the world. I am grateful for the opportunity to contribute to clinical research and remain motivated by the knowledge that every study is a collective effort to advance medicine and improve patient outcomes. My current work focuses on clinical research projects within China, although I have previously supported studies across the Asia-Pacific region, including Australia, New Zealand and South Korea. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I joined Fortrea in February 2017 through the first CRA Trainee Program in China, and over the past nine years I have built my career across a range of roles, progressing from CRA Trainee to CRA, Senior CRA, Clinical Team Lead, and Clinical Team Manager. I am now preparing to begin an exciting new chapter as a Project Manager. What is the best part of your job? What I enjoy most about my role is the opportunity to continuously learn, grow and contribute to the development of medicines that may improve patients' lives. One of the things that keeps clinical research so rewarding is that no two days are ever the same. Every study, site, and challenge presents an opportunity to learn something new. Throughout my career, I have gained experience across a wide range of therapeutic areas, including endocrinology, ophthalmology, infectious diseases, respiratory diseases, gynaecology, urology and nephrology. Along the way, I have developed not only technical experience but also leadership, project management, strategic thinking and cross-functional collaboration skills through working with teams around the world. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of the most fascinating aspects of clinical research is the diversity of people and experiences it brings. Throughout my career, I have had the opportunity to work with patients, investigators, site staff, sponsors and global study teams across many different therapeutic areas. Each study comes with its own scientific and operational challenges, which keeps the work engaging and intellectually stimulating. What has impressed me most is the dedication and resilience of clinical trial participants. Many patients face significant health challenges, yet they willingly contribute their time and effort not only for their own treatment options but also to help advance medical science for future generations. Their commitment is a constant source of inspiration. I have also been privileged to witness the continued growth and innovation within China's clinical research ecosystem, driven by the dedication of investigators, coordinators and site teams across the country. What are you most proud of in your work? I am proud of the professional journey I have built through continuous learning, growth and embracing new challenges. Starting my career with limited industry experience, Fortrea has given me the opportunity to develop through hands-on project work, mentorship and collaboration with talented colleagues. Adapting successfully to different roles, from monitoring activities as a CRA to leading study teams and managing complex projects, has required ongoing learning and personal development. Those experiences have shaped me into the professional I am today and reinforced the importance of remaining curious, adaptable, and committed to growth. What continues to motivate me is knowing that there is always another opportunity to learn and contribute. I am proud to be part of a team united by a shared purpose: helping bring innovative therapies to patients. Looking back on the past nine years, I am grateful for the opportunities, support and global perspective that Fortrea has provided, and I am excited to continue growing and contributing to the future of clinical research. articles.summary: By Tyler Thomas, Engineering Manager In commercial AI, eighteen months is an eternity. Microarchitectures turn over, memory bandwidth doubles, and rack-level thermal envelopes are rewritten before the thermal paste on last year’s deployment has even dried. In aerospace and defense, eighteen months may not get you through preliminary design reviews and initial environmental screening. This cadence mismatch is the central dilemma of modern tactical computing: Defense programs often run on 5- to 10-year lifecycles, but modern edge processing operates on an 18-month commercial silicon clock. If you design a mission system around a monolithic custom compute architecture, you are virtually guaranteed to field a legacy system. By the time an armored vehicle or an airborne ISR pod enters operational service, the deep neural networks it was intended to run have evolved past the compute capability of the silicon bolted inside it. Yet, simply buying commodity enterprise servers is typically a non-starter. A commercial datacenter box shaken on a tactical vehicle will shear connections, choke on dust, and succumb to dirty power transients within hours. articles.summary: Kaiyue Zhao harshitha.rv Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:02 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Beijing, China, supporting research sites in Beijing, Shenyang, Harbin, Chifeng, Weifang and Haikou. Depending on project needs, I also collaborate with sites and study teams across other regions of China. Working with sites throughout the country allows me to experience different research environments, build strong relationships with site teams and develop a broader perspective on clinical research in China. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have worked in clinical research since graduating from university in 2018. I joined Fortrea, formerly Covance, as a Study Start-Up specialist in December 2018 before transitioning into a Clinical Research Associate role in 2020. Since then, I have gained experience across different functions and contributed to a variety of clinical studies. It is rewarding to see innovative therapies progress through development and know that my work may help bring new treatment options to patients. What is the best part of your job? The best part of my role is contributing to the development of new medicines that may improve patients’ lives. Although I am not directly involved in treating patients or conducting laboratory research, I play an important role in supporting the quality, integrity and compliance of clinical studies. Every detail matters when turning scientific ideas into potential therapies. I also value the opportunity to learn continuously and collaborate with investigators, study coordinators, sponsors and colleagues across different teams. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of my most memorable experiences took place during a Pre-Study Visit with a Principal Investigator who was also the president of a major hospital. During the visit, I saw first-hand how he balanced patient care, clinical research, hospital operations and public responsibilities while remaining fully engaged in the study. A patient attending the clinic that day was also a surgeon who had travelled from another city for his advice. Watching their interaction reminded me that clinical research is about more than protocols and data. It is about people, their dedication and their shared commitment to advancing medicine. What are you most proud of in your work? I am proud of the work I do supporting sites and study teams in delivering high-quality clinical research while keeping patient safety and data integrity at the centre of everything we do. Clinical research is a team effort, and my role gives me the opportunity to connect different stakeholders, help solve challenges and support sites throughout the study lifecycle. How can business owners and employees begin using AI without being overwhelmed by the technology? In this Paychex THRIVE podcast episode, AI and innovation speaker Dan Chuparkoff joins host Gene Marks to discuss AI adoption, experimentation, and practical ways businesses can begin using AI assistants. The conversation explores what “using AI” can mean in everyday work, how to think about connecting AI tools to business data, privacy and permissions considerations, opportunities for small businesses to build AI applications, and examples of AI-assisted knowledge retrieval and conversation capture. The episode also examines whether imperfect business data limits AI use and how AI can provide feedback as a coach. articles.summary: Zhao Yi harshitha.rv@f… Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:13 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Taiyuan, Shanxi, China. Over the past five years at Fortrea, I have supported monitoring activities across clinical research sites throughout China, working with a wide range of investigators, site teams, and study stakeholders. These experiences have given me a broad perspective on clinical research operations and allowed me to build strong relationships while contributing to the successful delivery of studies across different regions. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have been working in clinical research for eight years, gaining experience in monitoring, site management and study execution across a variety of therapeutic areas and research settings. What is the best part of your job? One of the things I enjoy most about being a Clinical Research Associate is seeing how a clinical trial comes together through the efforts of many different people. The role requires a combination of scientific knowledge, attention to detail, communication skills and project awareness. Understanding complex protocols, identifying key details within source documentation, and working closely with investigators, site staff, sponsors and study teams all play an important part in helping studies progress. What makes the role especially rewarding is knowing that every monitoring visit, discussion and issue resolved contributes to the development of potential new therapies for patients. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? What I find most interesting about clinical research is the people behind every study. Each participant has a unique story, and I am always impressed by the dedication shown by both patients and their families. Many participants join clinical trials not only in the hope of accessing new treatment options, but also because they want to contribute to medical progress and help future patients. Their commitment is inspiring and serves as a constant reminder that behind every protocol, data point and study milestone are real people placing their trust in clinical research. What are you most proud of in your work? I am most proud of the moments when a study reaches an important milestone. Clinical trials require significant planning, coordination and collaboration over many years. Whether it is site activation, enrollment completion, database lock, or overall study completion, each achievement represents meaningful progress toward bringing innovative treatments to patients. Being part of that journey is what continues to motivate me and reinforces the importance of the work we do every day. I'm grateful for the opportunities I have had throughout my career and remain motivated by the chance to contribute to research that may ultimately improve patients' lives and advance the future of medicine. Clinical Trial Manager Site ConnectionsZhaoYiOff

articles.summary: Impact of Native American Scholarship Program Reflected in Past, Current Recipients mboyle Tue, 11/03/2026 - 08:01 Post Image November 3, 2026 - As Native American Heritage Month begins, Freeport is recognizing students who have used our Native American Scholarship Program to pursue educational and professional opportunities in their communities and beyond. Among them are two recipients at very different points in their careers: one just beginning her education with hopes of serving Native American communities through healthcare, and another now working as a nurse in the UK. Working with partners like Education Forward Arizona, Freeport helps create educational opportunities in the communities in which the company operates. Through the Native American Scholarship Program, eligible students can receive financial support as they pursue higher education. “For more than a decade, our Native American Scholarship Programs have opened doors that many of our students once thought were out of reach,” said Ondrea Barber, Manager-Global Indigenous Affairs & Human Rights. “With over $7 million invested and more than 550 scholarships awarded, we’ve helped Native American students become nurses, engineers, teachers and leaders who are giving back to their own communities and making a positive impact on the world.” Among the more recent recipients is Maureen Ford. A member of the Navajo Nation, Ford is a junior at Emory University in Atlanta and a recipient of the 2026-2027 Native American scholarship. Pursuing a bachelor's degree in human health, Ford hopes to one day build a career in healthcare leadership through organizations such as the Indian Health Service or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Passionate about improving healthcare access, strengthening public health programs and increasing Native American representation in health data and research, Ford plans to earn a Master of Public Health after completing her undergraduate studies and is considering medical school. She said a strong foundation in public health can create opportunities to improve health outcomes in Native communities and beyond. And Ford isn't alone when it comes to advancing the health of communities – whether it's those we're born into or the ones we eventually come to call home. For Shasha Tenijieth, the daughter of a Freeport employee and a member of both the San Carlos Apache and White Mountain Apache tribes, the Native American Scholarship Program helped support an educational journey that stretched far beyond Arizona. Finding scholarships that would support a student attending university outside the United States wasn’t always easy, Tenijieth said. Through the Native American Scholarship Program, however, she was able to pursue a degree in pediatric nursing and even complete an elective placement in East Africa before graduating from the University of Salford in the United Kingdom. She remains there today, where she now works as a pediatric cardiac nurse. Looking back, Tenijieth said the scholarship provided more than financial assistance. “The scholarship opened doors for me,” Tenijieth said. “Programs like Freeport’s relieve a lot of the financial stress and allow students to focus on their studies. Thanks to that, I had the opportunity to follow my passions, study internationally and build a career doing what I love.” Photos (top to bottom): A junior at Emory University, Maureen Ford hopes to one day have a career with Indian Health Service or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; After attending college in the UK, Shasha Tenijieth now lives and works there as a pediatric cardiac nurse.
articles.title: Impact of Native American Scholarship Program Reflected in Past, Current Recipients

articles.summary: Jian Cui harshitha.rv Tue, 11/03/2026 - 09:27 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Suzhou, China, a city known for its classical gardens. I oversee clinical research projects across China, with regional coverage extending to Japan and Southeast Asia, including the Philippines and Malaysia. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have worked in clinical research for more than 11 years. I began my career as a Clinical Research Associate in 2015 and joined the company, then known as Covance, as a CRA II in 2018. Since then, I have progressed through Senior CRA and Clinical Team Lead roles to my current position as Project Manager, overseeing projects from start to finish. What is the best part of your job? Clinical research is a highly planned discipline, with responsibilities and timelines carefully mapped out. This suits the way I like to work, as I genuinely enjoy bringing structure to complex projects and keeping everything organised. What I value most is bringing colleagues from different specialties together as one team, working towards a shared goal and supporting their development along the way. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of the most interesting aspects of my work has been visiting study sites in different cities and collaborating directly with experienced clinical professionals across a range of therapeutic areas. These experiences have allowed me to explore new approaches and potential treatments for disease. I have also been struck by how many patients, particularly in oncology, are still young yet face serious illnesses. This reinforces why our work matters and the importance of helping better treatments reach patients sooner. What are you most proud of in your work? I am most proud that my work creates value for both sponsors and patients. Delivering a study successfully from start to finish depends on getting countless details right. When a trial progresses smoothly and a new treatment has the opportunity to reach patients sooner, all the effort feels worthwhile. Project Manager Site ConnectionsJianCuiOff
articles.title: Jian Cui

articles.summary: Huijie Lv harshitha.rv Tue, 11/03/2026 - 09:18 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Shanghai, China, supporting clinical research sites across Shanghai, Zhejiang, Sichuan, and Shandong How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have worked in clinical research for more than six years and have had the opportunity to collaborate with investigators, study teams and healthcare professionals across a variety of sites, therapeutic areas and clinical trial phases. What is the best part of your job? What I enjoy the most about my role is the opportunity to work closely with investigators and site teams to help clinical trials run smoothly. Building strong relationships and maintaining open communication are important parts of my work, and I find it rewarding to collaborate with teams who share the same commitment to quality and patient care. At Fortrea, I value our focus on delivering high-quality clinical trials, and I take pride in knowing that our dedication, attention to detail and sense of responsibility help studies progress in a compliant and efficient manner. Ultimately, these efforts contribute to the development of new therapies that may provide additional treatment options for patients in the future. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of the most interesting aspects of clinical research has been seeing how awareness of clinical trials continues to grow among patients. Over the years, I have met many participants who actively choose to take part in studies because they hope to access new treatment options and contribute to medical progress. Their commitment and willingness to follow study requirements leave a lasting impression. I am also continually inspired by the dedication of investigators, medical staff and site teams, who consistently prioritize patient safety while working closely together to ensure studies are conducted according to protocol. These collaborations highlight the collective effort required to bring clinical research to life. What are you most proud of in your work? I am proud to support high-quality trial execution across a diverse range of sites, study phases and therapeutic areas. Clinical research requires careful oversight, problem-solving and continuous collaboration, and I take great satisfaction in helping teams overcome challenges and maintain study quality. Every issue resolved, every milestone achieved and every process improved contributes to protecting participant safety and maintaining the integrity of the research. I’m continually motivated by the purpose behind the work we do every day. Clinical research is about much more than processes and data - it’s about helping advance medical knowledge, supporting the development of innovative treatments and ultimately making a difference for patients. Knowing that my work contributes to that larger goal is what makes this career so meaningful and rewarding. Clinical Research Associate Site ConnectionsHuijieLvOff

articles.summary: Sainan Pei harshitha.rv Tue, 11/03/2026 - 11:08 Where are you located? What geographical region(s) do you cover? I am based in Shenyang, Liaoning Province, China. How long have you been working in the area of clinical research? I have been working in clinical research for eight years, including the past five years with Fortrea, supporting studies across all regions of China. Throughout my career, I have had the opportunity to work on a wide range of clinical trial projects, gaining experience across different therapeutic areas and collaborating with investigators, study teams and healthcare professionals nationwide. What is the best part of your job? What I enjoy most about my role as a Clinical Research Associate is the opportunity to contribute throughout the entire lifecycle of a clinical trial. My work includes preparing sites for study initiation, coordinating with investigators, overseeing trial procedures, conducting monitoring visits, verifying source data, and following up on study-related issues. While much of the role requires careful attention to detail and strong process management, I find it incredibly rewarding because every activity contributes to the quality and integrity of the research. Over the years, this work has strengthened my communication, problem-solving and critical thinking skills, while also teaching me the importance of precision, accountability and collaboration. What has been interesting about your work in clinical research? Did anything surprise you about the patient population? One of the most fascinating aspects of clinical research is that it is a profession built on continuous learning. Every study presents an opportunity to deepen my understanding of medical science, drug development and industry regulations. I have worked alongside experienced investigators, physicians and healthcare teams, gaining valuable insights into how clinical research is translated into real-world medical practice. The dynamic nature of the field means there is always something new to learn, whether it is an innovative treatment approach, an emerging therapeutic area or an evolving regulatory requirement. What are you most proud of in your work? What I am most proud of is maintaining a strong commitment to quality throughout every study I support. Clinical trial data must be accurate, complete and compliant, as these factors are essential to protecting patients and advancing scientific knowledge. In my daily work, I carefully review data, follow up on issues, assess potential risks and work closely with investigators and site teams to help ensure studies progress smoothly. I take pride in knowing that my attention to detail helps contribute to the reliability of clinical research and supports the development of new treatments. Perhaps the most meaningful part of my work is knowing that clinical trials have the potential to improve patients' lives. Being able to contribute, even in a small way, to the journey of a medicine from clinical development to real-world use is something I never take for granted. That sense of purpose continues to motivate me every day and remains one of the most rewarding aspects of a career in clinical research. Senior Clinical Research Associate Site ConnectionsSainanPeiOff
articles.title: Sainan Pei

How AI Can Help Small Businesses Compete and Grow

How can small businesses think about AI, economic conditions, and growth opportunities? In this Paychex THRIVE podcast episode, host Gene Marks speaks with Kevin Hassett about tariffs, government and private-sector economic data, labor-market trends, and the role AI may play in small-business productivity and competitiveness. The conversation also discusses how businesses can interpret changing economic indicators and why AI is being closely watched for its potential impact on workers and firms. Explore current hiring and wage trends through the Paychex Small Business Employment Watch, learn more about AI for small businesses, or see how Paychex WISE brings AI-powered intelligence into workforce operations.

  • 17:22 - The Underreported Positive: Side Gigs & Extra Income
  • 20:00 - AI as a Small Business Game Changer
